analysis.one_liner: Strips all Endangered Species Act protection from the lesser prairie chicken and bans future listings.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the final month of 2022 with four Republican cosponsors, the bill never left committee and died when the Congress ended, leaving the bird's endangered and threatened listings in place.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would remove the lesser prairie chicken from the Endangered Species Act in Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas, Colorado, and New Mexico, where one population is listed as endangered and another as threatened. It would require the Interior Department to drop both listings within 60 days and would permanently bar the department from listing the bird again, no matter how small its population gets. In practice, this frees energy development and farming in the bird's grassland habitat from the checks the Endangered Species Act imposes.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas producers, wind and solar developers, and farmers and ranchers in the five-state region gain, because Endangered Species Act listings restrict activities — drilling, construction, turbine siting, plowing, and grazing — in the bird's habitat. Removing the listings and banning future ones eliminates the federal permitting, consultation, and land-use limits that come with a listed species.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Southern Plains energy and agricultural interests

how_it_helps.text: The bill orders the Interior Department to remove both existing populations — the Southern population (listed as endangered) and the Northern population (listed as threatened) — from the endangered and threatened species lists within 60 days of enactment.

It permanently forbids the Interior Department from listing any lesser prairie chicken population in Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas, Colorado, or New Mexico as threatened or endangered in the future, so no later administration could restore the protection through the normal scientific review process.

For energy companies and agricultural landowners, removing the bird from the Act's authority means no federal consultation requirements, no restrictions on take, and no habitat-based limits on drilling, construction, farming, or wind development in the bird's range.

analysis.who_pays: The public bears the cost: an at-risk grassland bird permanently loses its federal safety net, with no substitute federal protection, and citizens lose the Endangered Species Act's legal tools to check habitat destruction across parts of five states.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public and the bird itself

drawbacks.text: The bill strips protections that were already in effect — an endangered listing for the southern population and a threatened listing for the northern one — without putting any federal safeguard in their place.

The ban on future listings is absolute: even if the bird's numbers later collapse to the point where federal scientists would normally classify it as endangered, the Interior Department could not act in those five states.

Once the bird is outside the Act, citizens and conservation groups lose the ability to enforce habitat protections in court, and habitat loss from energy development and farming could proceed without a federal check.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real but narrow: less regulatory friction and cost for oil, gas, wind, and agricultural operations in the five-state range. The cost is permanent — a statutory guarantee that one of the region's most declining grassland birds can never regain federal protection, regardless of what the science shows. For anyone who values the Endangered Species Act's role as a backstop, this is a bad trade; even an honest supporter would have to acknowledge that the bill forecloses recovery options rather than funding them.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the last month of the session, referred to the Natural Resources Committee, and never moved — it expired when the Congress ended in early January 2023.

narrative.text: Representative Ron Estes introduced the bill on December 7, 2022, in the final weeks of the 117th Congress, with introductory remarks entered in the record.
It was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources the same day; no hearing, markup, or floor action ever followed.
Four House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.
When the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, the bill died, and the lesser prairie chicken's endangered and threatened listings remained in place.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The bird, and the public interest in keeping federal endangered-species protection available, came out ahead: the existing listings survived and no prohibition on future listings was enacted. The oil, gas, wind, and agricultural interests seeking relief from the listings gained nothing from this Congress, though they remain free to pursue the same outcome in the next one.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The bird and its federal protections

for.name: Rep. Ron Estes
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and entered introductory remarks in the record.

for.name: Southern Plains oil and gas and agricultural interests
for.role: Industry stakeholders in the lesser prairie chicken's five-state range
for.what_they_did: Widely reported to have opposed the 2022 listings and sought congressional action to undo them; this bill was written to that end.

against.name: House Committee on Natural Resources (Chair Raúl Grijalva)
against.role: Committee of referral; never scheduled a hearing or markup
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred on December 7, 2022, letting it expire at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all four cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democratic support; no vote was ever taken, so there is no roll-call record to measure the split.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers (Southern Plains and Permian Basin)
industries.note: Endangered Species Act listings restrict drilling and related construction in the bird's grassland habitat; the bill removes the listings and bans future ones, eliminating those federal limits. The savings accrue to operators, while the public loses the species protection the Act provides.

Renewable developers building across the five-state range face siting and take restrictions where the bird is listed; the bill removes that constraint. The public cost is the loss of habitat protection.

Listings can limit plowing, grazing, and land conversion in habitat areas; the bill frees agricultural landowners from those requirements. Their gain comes at the direct expense of the species' federal protection.
